reference_title: Design and Construction of Continuous Flight Auger Piles

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: CFA piles have been used little on transportation projects, partly from perceived QC difficulties and because proprietary DD systems fit design-bid-build poorly. The Chapter 8 performance-based specification makes the contractor set pile lengths and provide QC and performance measurements; the chapter reviews QA/QC practice and gives recommended best practices, summarized in 7.7.
sections.body: CFA piles have a history of U.S. commercial use but have been used infrequently on public transportation projects, at least partly because of perceived quality control difficulties, and proprietary DD systems are not easily fitted into design-bid-build delivery. The Chapter 8 guide specification is performance-based: the contractor determines final pile lengths and provides the quality control and performance measurements that assure the owner of capacity and integrity; the key is that the specifications require measurements giving a reliable indication of performance, which lets contractors seek the most cost-effective and timely solutions. The chapter reviews QA/QC practice in the U.S. and abroad, includes recommended best practices in each section and summarizes them in the last section. (p. 160)
key_points: Perceived QC difficulties have limited CFA use on transportation projects (p. 160).
Chapter 8's performance-based specification makes the contractor set final pile lengths (p. 160).
Specifications must require measurements that reliably indicate performance (p. 160).
sections.applicability: QC/QA framework for CFA piles under a performance-based specification

sections.title: The Role of the Inspector
sections.summary: The inspector must understand CFA installation, verify good practice and understand the automated and manual data, ensuring data are collected (and perhaps duplicating manual data). Recommended records: 21 items including location, depths, reinforcement, flow cone or slump and volumes, times, weather, samples, and automated readings every 0.6 m (2 ft) or less of rotation, volume and pressures.
sections.body: The inspector has a significant role in observing and recording the contractor's QA/QC: much testing, automated data and manual data are recorded, and the inspector must (a) understand CFA installation fundamentals, (b) verify good construction practice and (c) understand the data collected, possibly also collecting manual data to duplicate or back up the contractor's. Even where the contractor records data, the inspector must ensure it is collected; agencies' protocols divide responsibilities (p. 160). Recommended records: location and plumbness; ground elevation; toe depth; top of grout/concrete; pile length; auger diameter; reinforcement details; flow cone efflux time and grout volume, or slump and concrete volume; theoretical excavation volume (auger diameter); depth of reinforcement; dates and times of drilling, mixing, truck arrival (with batch tickets), pumping and reinforcement placement; weather and air temperature; sample identification; other pertinent data (p. 161); and all automated readings, at minimum auger rotation vs. depth and volume vs. outlet depth for every 0.6 m (2 ft) or less, average maximum and minimum pump stroke pressures at ground level and, if directed, near the auger head, and, if specified, torque and crowd force during drilling (p. 162). (pp. 160 to 162)
key_points: Inspector must understand CFA installation, verify good practice and understand the data (p. 160).
Inspector must ensure data are collected even when the contractor records them (p. 160).
Records include volumes vs. depth, flow cone or slump, times, weather and samples (p. 161).
Automated readings every 0.6 m (2 ft) or less: rotation, volume, pump pressures; torque and crowd if specified (pp. 161 to 162).
sections.applicability: Inspector responsibilities and pre-construction planning for CFA pile projects

sections.title: Pre-Construction Planning
sections.summary: QA/QC begins with planning: under the performance-based model the contractor submits design calculations, working drawings, a pile installation plan and a conformance testing plan for owner review; the owner supplies preliminary design information, and the contractor designs piles and cap connections and selects process and equipment, with a preliminary design at bid.
sections.body: Effective QA/QC begins with planning. Under the performance-based specification the contractor submits design calculations, working drawings, a detailed pile installation plan and a conformance testing plan for review by the owner, engineers and inspectors, and the owner provides information for the contractor's design and plans. In the Chapter 8 method the owner provides preliminary design information and the contractor designs the individual piles and pile cap connections and selects the process and equipment; qualified contractors submit a preliminary design with the bid, and after award the selected contractor submits detailed calculations and working drawings for review. (p. 162)
key_points: Contractor submits design calculations, working drawings, installation plan and testing plan (p. 162).
Owner provides preliminary design information; contractor designs piles and cap connections (p. 162).
A preliminary design is submitted with the bid; details after award (p. 162).
sections.applicability: Inspector responsibilities and pre-construction planning for CFA pile projects

sections.title: Owner-Supplied Information
sections.summary: Owner-supplied pre-bid information: plans with design loads, minimum diameter, tip elevation, minimum reinforcement, cap connection and layout; design criteria (loads, allowable displacements, safety factor); geotechnical reports; site information; material and testing requirements; and submittal requirements. The factual geotechnical report should be part of the contract special provisions.
sections.body: The owner should provide preliminary design information pre-bid, generally: (1) plans with pile design loadings, minimum diameter, tip elevation, minimum reinforcement, pile to footing/cap connection and layout; (2) design criteria and requirements (design loads, maximum allowable displacements, safety factor); (3) geotechnical reports with borings, test pits and other subsurface data near the piles; (4) site information (right-of-way, utilities, site limitations) (p. 162); (5) material and testing requirements for grout/concrete and reinforcement; and (6) submittal and review requirements. Subsurface conditions strongly affect the contractor's choices, bidding and administration; the geotechnical report should be a factual document included in the contract special provisions, alerting bidders and reducing differing site condition claims, and thereby becomes a legal part of the contract (p. 163). (pp. 162 to 163)
key_points: Owner supplies loads, minimum diameter, tip elevation, minimum reinforcement and layout (p. 162).
Design criteria include allowable displacements and safety factor (p. 162).
Include the factual geotechnical report in the contract special provisions (p. 163).
sections.applicability: Inspector responsibilities and pre-construction planning for CFA pile projects

sections.title: CFA Contractor Experience
sections.summary: CFA pile quality depends on the contractor and crew; only experienced contractors should work, and all must build a test pile. Recommended: three similar successful projects in the prior two years; site supervisor, rig operators and project manager each with at least three years of CFA experience; personnel lists with documentation.
sections.body: CFA pile quality is highly dependent on the skill of the contractor and the specific crew, so the contractor must document successful prior projects of a similar nature; only experienced contractors will be allowed, and all will be required to construct a test pile. For transportation projects: (1) at least three projects with CFA piles installed successfully under similar conditions in the two years before the bid; (2) the job site supervisor with at least three years supervising CFA installation; (3) drill rig operators with at least three years installing CFA piles; (4) the project manager with at least three years on CFA projects of similar size and scope. A personnel list with documentation should be submitted. (p. 163)
key_points: Quality depends highly on the contractor's and crew's skill (p. 163).
All contractors should construct a test pile (p. 163).
Contractor: at least three similar successful CFA projects in the prior two years (p. 163).
Supervisor, rig operators and project manager: at least three years of CFA experience each (p. 163).
sections.applicability: Inspector responsibilities and pre-construction planning for CFA pile projects

sections.title: Design Submittals
sections.summary: CFA piles should be designed by a Professional Engineer licensed in the project's state, with at least three successful CFA projects of similar capacity in the past five years; field revisions are documented by revised calculations or drawings, and as-built drawings are recommended.
sections.body: The CFA piles shall be designed by a Professional Engineer (Design Engineer) licensed in the state of the project, with experience designing at least three successfully completed CFA pile projects over the past five years with piles of similar capacity (p. 163). Design revisions for field conditions are documented by revised calculations and/or working drawings, and as-built drawings are recommended on completion (p. 164). (pp. 163 to 164)
key_points: Design Engineer licensed in the project's state (p. 163).
Design Engineer: at least three successful CFA projects of similar capacity in the past five years (p. 163).
As-built drawings recommended on completion (p. 164).
sections.applicability: Inspector responsibilities and pre-construction planning for CFA pile projects

sections.title: Design Calculations
sections.summary: Design calculations should include a summary report, critical cross-sections with strata, water levels and loads, design criteria (strengths, unit weights, unit side and end resistances, extra subsurface data), safety factors, seismic criteria, indexed and signed calculation sheets, notes on symbols and programs, and pile to cap calculations.
sections.body: Design calculations should include at least: (1) a written summary report of the overall design; (2) critical design cross-sections with strata, piezometric levels and applied loads; (3) design criteria including strengths (friction angle and cohesion), unit weights, unit skin friction and unit end-bearing values, and any additional subsurface data collected; (4) safety factors; (5) seismic acceleration coefficient or other seismic criteria; (6) calculation sheets (static and seismic) with project number, location, designation, date, designer and checker initials and page numbers, with an index; (7) design notes explaining symbols and computer programs; and (8) pile to cap/footing calculations. (p. 164)
key_points: Include unit skin friction and end-bearing values and safety factors used (p. 164).
Calculation sheets indexed, with designer and checker initials (p. 164).
sections.applicability: Inspector responsibilities and pre-construction planning for CFA pile projects

sections.title: Working Drawings
sections.summary: Working drawings should show a plan view (baseline, offsets, stations, pile locations and spacing, right-of-way, utilities and structures, drainage, explorations), an elevation view, general construction notes, curve data, quantities, typical sections with reinforcement, centralizers and cap connections, test pile and reaction details, and pile and reinforcement schedules.
sections.body: Working drawings should include, unless in the contract plans: (1) a plan view with reference baseline, offsets at alignment changes, beginning and end stations, pile locations and center-to-center spacing (p. 164), right-of-way and easement limits, known utilities, adjacent structures or interferences, drainage structures or pipes, and subsurface exploration locations; (2) an elevation view with pile locations, elevations and spacing and existing and finish grades; (3) general construction notes including sequencing; (4) horizontal and vertical curve data and control points; (5) a summary of quantities; (6) typical sections with spacing, diameter, reinforcing details, centralizers and spacers, and connections to the footing/pile cap; (7) typical details of verification and proof load test piles with reaction systems; and (8) details, dimensions and schedules of all piles and reinforcing steel (p. 165). (pp. 164 to 165)
key_points: Plan view shows pile locations, spacing, utilities, structures and exploration locations (pp. 164 to 165).
Typical sections show reinforcement, centralizers, spacers and cap connections (p. 165).
Include verification and proof load test pile details with reaction systems (p. 165).
sections.applicability: Inspector responsibilities and pre-construction planning for CFA pile projects

sections.title: Pile Installation Plan
sections.summary: The pile installation plan demonstrates equipment, techniques and materials: equipment and calibration, procedures, sequence, target drilling and grouting parameters with ranges, reinforcement placement and centering, mix designs with slump loss and strength vs. time, monitoring equipment, contingency plans, and protection of adjacent structures. Review in about 14 days, scrutinizing rig capacity, torque, power and pump.
sections.body: The Pile Installation Plan demonstrates the acceptability of the contractor's equipment, techniques and materials, including at least: (1) proposed equipment (rigs, augers and tools, grout or concrete pumps, mixing and automated monitoring equipment) with calibration procedures; (2) step-by-step installation procedures; (3) the installation sequence (p. 165); (4) target drilling and grouting parameters with acceptable ranges (auger rotation speed, penetration rates, torque, crowd, grout pressures and grout volume factors); (5) reinforcement placement, support at the top and centering methods; (6) mix designs with slump loss and strength development vs. time (for fly ash and/or slag mixes); (7) monitoring of rotation speed, penetration rate, depth and crowd; (8) monitoring of grout or concrete pressures and volumes; (9) contingency plans for equipment failure; (10) protection of adjacent structures with a monitoring plan 'as required in Section 3.1'; and (11) other required submittals. A clear plan reduces misunderstandings and claims; the review period should be defined in the contract, 14 days being suitable for most routine projects. Key equipment items to scrutinize: rig rated capacity and boom lengths; torque, rotational speed and down crowd capacity; horsepower of the hydraulic power unit; and the positive displacement piston-ball valve grout pump's stroke displacements, horsepower and pressures; the plan should document that the drilling equipment has worked on similar piles in similar soils (p. 166). (pp. 165 to 166)
key_points: Target drilling and grouting parameters with acceptable ranges are part of the installation plan (p. 166).
Mix designs include slump loss and strength development vs. time curves (p. 166).
Contingency plans for grout pump or monitoring equipment failure are required (p. 166).
Review period defined in the contract; 14 days suits most routine projects (p. 166).
Scrutinize rig torque, speed, crowd, hydraulic power and grout pump capacity (p. 166).
Document that the drilling equipment worked on similar piles in similar soils (p. 166).
sections.applicability: Inspector responsibilities and pre-construction planning for CFA pile projects

sections.title: Testing Plan
sections.summary: The owner's contract testing plan, with the contractor's plan for performing it, includes pre-production static load tests, production static, rapid or dynamic tests and post-installation integrity tests, to show installed piles meet load and deflection criteria; production piles should match an accepted test pile, checked by automated monitoring, verification tests and integrity tests.
sections.body: The testing plan should be a contract requirement provided by the owner, the contractor including with the Pile Installation Plan a plan to construct and perform the tests. The program comprises pre-production static load tests, production static and/or rapid and/or dynamic load tests and post-installation integrity tests in sufficient numbers to show installed piles meet the load and deflection criteria with an appropriate factor of safety. Pre-production test piles establish or verify means, methods and capacity; production installation then ensures all production piles are the same as a test pile, evaluated pile by pile through automated monitoring, with verification load tests and integrity tests during construction. Sections 7.4 to 7.6 discuss each component. (p. 167)
key_points: Testing plan is an owner-provided contract requirement (p. 167).
Program: pre-production static tests, production static/rapid/dynamic tests, integrity tests (p. 167).
All production piles should be the same as an accepted test pile (p. 167).
sections.applicability: Inspector responsibilities and pre-construction planning for CFA pile projects

sections.title: Pre-Production Testing
sections.summary: Pre-production testing (one or more static tests, maybe lateral and uplift; for large projects one static test plus rapid or dynamic tests calibrated to it) uses piles built like production piles to set target penetration rates, pressure/volume relations (grout factor within +/-7.5% of the test pile's), torque and crowd for DD piles, mix parameters, and design correlations.
sections.body: Pre-production load testing generally comprises one or more static load tests depending on pile numbers, capacity range and subsurface variability; lateral and uplift tests may be included; very large projects may use one static test supplemented by rapid (usually Statnamic) or dynamic tests, calibrating them against the static test before production (Section 7.6). Test piles (and any reaction piles) should have all the construction, monitoring, testing and inspection requirements of production piles. Results are used to: (1) set target drilling penetration rates for the site's conditions; (2) set pressure/volume relations for placement, the grout factor (used over theoretical volume) of the test piles +/-7.5% being used for production piles (p. 167); (3) set target torque and crowd for displacement or partial displacement piles; (4) set mix parameters such as grout flow and admixtures; (5) evaluate design correlations of side and base resistance. Testing may run concurrently with the start of production to save mobilization, though design changes are then limited; on very large projects a separate mobilization may be justified (p. 168). (pp. 167 to 168)
key_points: Large projects: one static test plus rapid or dynamic tests calibrated to it (p. 167).
Test piles must meet all production construction, monitoring and inspection requirements (p. 167).
Production grout factor: the test pile's value +/-7.5% (p. 167).
Set target torque and crowd for displacement or partial displacement piles (p. 168).
Concurrent pre-production testing saves mobilization but limits design changes (p. 168).
sections.applicability: Inspector responsibilities and pre-construction planning for CFA pile projects

sections.title: Conformance Monitoring and Verification Tests
sections.summary: Conformance: automated monitoring (contract requirement) of rotation, injection point depth, torque and crowd in drilling, and volume, maximum and minimum pressure, rotation and depth in grouting, calibrated within 3%; integrity tests (sonic echo for small piles, downhole tubes over 760 mm); verification tests on at least 2% of production piles (one or two on projects under about 50 piles).
sections.body: Conformance monitoring uses automated recording to confirm installation criteria, integrity testing and verification tests on production piles. Automated monitoring gives real-time evaluation of each pile and is a contract requirement; the installation plan gives equipment type, manufacturer, data, current calibration and sample records. Drilling minimum: auger rotation, injection point depth, torque and crowd force, all against injection point depth (rotational and position indicators, load cells on the auger head) (p. 168); grouting minimum: volume, maximum and minimum pressure, rotation if rotated and injection depth (flowmeters, pressure transducers, position and rotation indicators). Equipment is calibrated at project start per the manufacturer, values within three percent. Integrity tests: down-tube methods (crosshole and single-hole sonic, backscatter gamma, fiber-optic camera) are most reliable but costly and generally impractical for piles under 760 mm (30 in.); sonic echo from the top suits routine checks of the upper 10 to 20 diameters; piles with abnormal records can be integrity or load tested; frequency is given in 'Section 7.3.3' (as printed). Verification tests on at least two percent of production piles, or one or two on projects under about 50 piles depending on variability and experience, by static, rapid or dynamic tests, also to accept or reject questionable piles (p. 169); periodic tests confirm techniques keep giving adequate capacity, and rapid or dynamic results should be calibrated to static tests in pre-production unless comparisons exist from similar soils (p. 170). (pp. 168 to 170)
key_points: Automated monitoring is a contract requirement (p. 168).
Drilling: rotation, injection depth, torque and crowd vs. depth (p. 168).
Grouting: volume, maximum and minimum pressure, rotation and injection depth (pp. 168 to 169).
Monitoring equipment calibrated to within three percent (p. 169).
Down-tube integrity tests generally impractical for piles under 760 mm (30 in.) (p. 169).
Verification tests on at least 2% of production piles; one or two on projects under about 50 piles (p. 169).
Calibrate rapid or dynamic tests to static tests in pre-production (p. 170).
sections.applicability: Inspector responsibilities and pre-construction planning for CFA pile projects

sections.title: Materials Testing
sections.summary: Grout and concrete sampling and testing requirements (type and frequency) belong in the owner's bid package, referencing State DOT standard specifications; testing may be by the owner, a contractor's independent firm, or both.
sections.body: Sampling and testing requirements for grout and concrete should be in the owner's bid package, referencing the State DOT Standard Specifications plus any additional contractor testing, with test type and frequency. Testing may be by the owner, an independent firm working for the contractor, or both, as the specifications state; see Chapter 4 and Section 7.4. (p. 170)
key_points: Materials testing type and frequency in the owner's bid package (p. 170).
sections.applicability: Inspector responsibilities and pre-construction planning for CFA pile projects

sections.title: Performance Monitoring and Control During Construction
sections.summary: CFA construction is hidden, so visual observation and estimated volumes are insufficient for transportation QA/QC; automated measurements give operators control and owners documentation. Automated monitoring is not the sole record: inspectors note pile top completion, cage installation and problems, and check the equipment manually; stop installation if it malfunctions.
sections.body: CFA construction is hidden from operator and inspector; past practice relied on a skilled operator's visual observations and inaccurate estimates of grout pumped. Skilled operators and experienced contractors matter, but visual observation alone is insufficient for transportation QA/QC; technology gives operators information for judgment and control and gives inspectors and owners documentation of proper practice (equipment in Chapter 4). Automated monitoring should not be the sole record: also needed are visual records of pile top completion, workmanship of clearing debris and forming the top, cage installation, and difficulties and their resolution; the inspector should periodically check the automated data manually, the level of duplication depending on the agency and project. If the automated equipment malfunctions during production, installation should stop until repaired. (p. 170)
key_points: Visual observation alone is insufficient QA/QC for transportation projects (p. 170).
Automated monitoring is not the sole record; manual and visual records supplement it (p. 170).
Inspector periodically checks automated data manually (p. 170).
Stop pile installation if the automated equipment malfunctions (p. 170).
sections.applicability: Real-time monitoring and control requirements during CFA pile drilling, grouting, and reinforcement installation

sections.title: Monitoring and Control of the Drilling Phase
sections.summary: Drilling control prevents excessive flighting (CFA) and ensures displacement (DD): record depth, speed, penetration rate and torque. Table 7.1: 2 to 3 revolutions per pitch in clay, 1.5 to 2 in cohesionless soils; the faster rate controls in mixed profiles. Manual stopwatch control is insufficient; cab displays with depth encoder and revolution counter (Figure 7.1) are required for DD piles and CFA piles in non-cohesive soils.
sections.body: Drilling should be controlled so conventional CFA piles avoid excessive flighting and DD piles get the right displacement; operator and inspector observe and record auger depth, speed, penetration rate and torque. The contractor estimates the penetration rate in design and the installation plan; Table 7.1 gives experience guidelines, affected by factors such as flight pitch; pre-production piles confirm or adjust it, and production piles use the test piles' practices unless conditions change significantly (p. 171). In mixed profiles the higher penetration rate (fewer revolutions) should control, since the clay rate could cause excessive flighting of sand; for partial displacement piles the rate governs displacement and strongly affects axial resistance; for full displacement piles it is set by the need to displace soil. The manual commercial system (gearbox speed, observing the auger top in the leads, stopwatch) is not sufficiently accurate for transportation projects and should only check or back up automated systems. The recommended system uses a depth encoder and revolution counter displaying revolutions per meter (or foot) to the operator and recording it (p. 171), usually on hydraulic fixed-mast rigs with control of crowd, torque and speed (Figure 7.1); the cab display and monitoring are required for DD piles and for CFA piles in non-cohesive soils; CFA piles may be installed without drilling monitoring and control only in soils shown to be non-caving and not subject to flighting. Crane-mounted rigs have no crowd beyond dead weight; their encoder-and-clock record is acceptable only for non-critical foundations such as soundwalls at shallow depth in favorable soils (p. 172). (pp. 171 to 172)
key_points: Record auger depth, speed, penetration rate and torque during drilling (p. 171).
Table 7.1: clay 2 to 3, cohesionless 1.5 to 2 revolutions per auger pitch (p. 171).
In mixed profiles the higher penetration rate (fewer revolutions) controls (p. 171).
Production piles use the successful test piles' practices unless conditions change (p. 171).
Manual stopwatch control is not sufficiently accurate for transportation projects (p. 171).
Cab display and monitoring required for DD piles and CFA piles in non-cohesive soils (p. 172).
Crane-rig encoder-and-clock records acceptable only for non-critical shallow foundations (p. 172).

sections.title: Monitoring and Control of the Grouting/Concreting Phase
sections.summary: Grouting control may be the most important QA/QC aspect: monitor pressure and volume vs. depth, establish flow with a 150 to 300 mm lift, over-supply the lowest 0.9 to 1.8 m about twice, pull steadily under pressure, and re-drill 1.5 m below a pressure drop. Automated monitoring (position sensor, in-line flowmeter, pressure near the swivel or tip, rotation, cab display) is recommended; stroke counting is inferior.
sections.body: Control of grouting/concreting may be the most important QA/QC aspect: adequate grout or concrete must reach the auger's discharge point at proper pressure, or the pile may fail geotechnically or structurally (pp. 172 to 173). Pressure and volume must be monitored vs. auger depth, and extraction should be slow and continuous without excessive or reverse rotation. At tip elevation, flow is established with minimal lift, typically 150 to 300 mm (6 to 12 in.); after the plug blows, an initial charge builds pressure before lifting; the lowest 0.9 to 1.8 m (3 to 6 ft) should get about twice the theoretical volume. The auger is pulled smoothly at steady speed with continuous pumping (some rotate slowly in the drilling direction); tip position, lifting speed, volume and pressure are documented; if pressure drops below allowable levels, a common practice is to re-drill 1.5 m (5 ft) below the drop and rebuild from there. The manual method (auger height in the leads, stopwatch, counted pump strokes, gauge near the pump) documents only through the inspector's notes (p. 173) and is not sufficient for transportation projects, serving as a check or for non-critical shallow foundations. The recommended automated system gives tip position (sensor, Figure 7.2), volume by in-line flowmeter (Figure 7.3), pressure near the swivel or, better, in the auger near the tip, rotation, lifting speed against displayed targets, and a full record; pressure-pulse stroke counting is inferior to a flowmeter, and a gauge near the pump is least effective. Hydraulic pressure sensors (Figure 7.4) document torque and crowd, useful for DD piles (p. 174). The inspector's display (Figure 7.5) and an example record (Figure 7.6: 17% over-consumption vs. a 15% target, 15% to 20% typical for CFA piles; a harder layer at about 46 to 54 ft shown by higher torque and thrust) illustrate the documentation (p. 176). (pp. 172 to 177)
key_points: Grouting control may be the most important part of CFA QA/QC (p. 172).
Establish flow with minimal lift, typically 150 to 300 mm (6 to 12 in.) (p. 173).
Lowest 0.9 to 1.8 m (3 to 6 ft): about twice the theoretical volume (p. 173).
After a pressure drop, a common practice is to re-drill 1.5 m (5 ft) below it and rebuild (p. 173).
Manual monitoring is not sufficient control for transportation projects (p. 174).
In-line flowmeter preferred; pressure best measured in the auger near the tip, next near the swivel (p. 174).
Over-consumption of 15% to 20% is typical for CFA piles (p. 176).

sections.title: Finishing the Pile Top and Installing Reinforcement
sections.summary: Pile top and reinforcement depend on the inspector: note where grout first appears (over about 3 m up the flights suggests an uncharged auger) and keep flow steady after venting; dip out contamination, use a small surface casing; place clean reinforcement with non-metal centralizers by gravity or a gentle push, support it for hours; record shortfalls.
sections.body: Reinforcement installation and pile top completion are not automatically monitored and depend on the inspector. Note where grout/concrete appears at the surface relative to the auger tip: rising more than about 3 m (10 ft) up the flights may mean the auger did not stay charged with soil; the point should be consistent pile to pile; once vented, positive tip pressure is lost, so flow must stay consistent. Spilled soil must be dipped out and the pile finished with good material (Figures 7.7, 7.8); a small surface casing is normally required. Reinforcement follows immediately, clean and rust-free, with plastic or mortar centering devices, never metal; welding only of weldable steel (p. 178). It is lowered by gravity or a gentle push (Figure 7.9), not driven, hammered or vibrated unless permitted (vibration normally only for fully welded cages); a cage short of depth is recorded and the engineer notified; the cage is supported at the surface for typically a few hours. Loss of workability or dewatering in sands can hinder placement; anti-washout or viscosity modifying admixtures may help. Rebar beyond 18 m (60 ft) is possible in favorable conditions, though large bending rarely occurs that deep. Below-grade cutoffs are made by excavating, chipping and cutting rebar, or, in cohesive soils within a few feet of the surface, by dipping the fluid grout with a surface casing (p. 179). (pp. 178 to 180)
key_points: Grout rising more than about 3 m (10 ft) up the flights may mean the auger was not charged with soil (p. 178).
Once grout vents at the surface, keep flow consistent so the auger is not pulled too fast (p. 178).
A small surface casing is normally required at the top of the hole (p. 178).
Centering devices plastic or mortar, never metal (p. 178).
Do not drive, hammer or vibrate reinforcement unless permitted (p. 179).
Record a cage that cannot reach full depth and notify the engineer (p. 179).
Dipping to a below-grade cutoff requires a surface casing (p. 179).

sections.title: Sampling and Testing of the Grout or Concrete
sections.summary: The contractor owns the mix; the inspector samples to verify. Concrete: 150 x 300 mm cylinders, typically 24 to 31 MPa (3,000 to 4,500 psi) as printed, six samples per 40 m3 and at least one set per day; slump 200 +/- 25 mm on every truck. Grout: 50 mm cubes (10% higher requirement), flow cone with a 19 mm opening, 10 to 25 s, on every truck, kept for two hours. Site water only as approved.
sections.body: Sampling and testing are by or under the inspector; the mix is the contractor's responsibility and samples verify requirements; strength is the design control and workability is checked in the field (p. 180). Concrete: 150 mm (6 in.) by 300 mm (12 in.) cylinders (ASTM C31), tested per ASTM C39; strengths typically 24 to 31 MPa (3,000 to 4,500 psi), as printed; at least six samples per 40 m3 (about 50 yd3), and at least one set per day or batch (p. 180). Grout: 50 mm (2 in.) cubes (ASTM C109, Figure 7.10); pea-gravel mixes are concrete; extra samples help since small cubes test low if misaligned; 75 x 150 mm or 50 x 100 mm cylinders need attention to aggregate size and height-to-diameter ratio and a correlation to the mix design method; cube requirements are typically 10% above cylinder values. Slump (ASTM C143) on each truck, about 200 +/- 25 mm (8 +/- 1 in.); slump loss vs. time in the mix design; mixes should keep slump or flow at least two hours on routine projects, with warm-weather adjustments. Site water only per the approved plan or engineer's approval, within the design water-cementitious ratio, as a rare exception, with samples after adding (p. 181). Grout flow cone tests on each truck; ASTM C939 or USACE CRD 611-94, modified from the 12 mm (0.5 in.) outlet to a 19 mm (0.75 in.) opening; suitable grouts have efflux times of 10 to 25 seconds (p. 182) maintained for at least two hours and never less than the time to complete a pile and place reinforcement (p. 183). (pp. 180 to 183)
key_points: Mix design is the contractor's responsibility; the inspector samples to verify (p. 180).
Concrete strength typically 24 to 31 MPa (3,000 to 4,500 psi), as printed (p. 180).
At least six samples per 40 m3 (about 50 yd3) and one set per day (p. 180).
Grout cubes 50 mm (2 in.); cube strength requirement typically 10% above cylinders (p. 181).
Slump on each truck, about 200 +/- 25 mm (8 +/- 1 in.) (p. 181).
Keep slump or flow at least two hours on routine projects (p. 181).
Flow cone with 19 mm (0.75 in.) opening; efflux 10 to 25 s for at least two hours (pp. 182 to 183).

sections.title: Post-Construction Integrity Testing
sections.summary: Post-construction integrity tests supplement installation monitoring to show the contractor's procedures give acceptable piles; methods mostly come from drilled shaft practice (O'Neill and Reese, 1999; DFI, 2005).
sections.body: Post-construction integrity tests supplement installation monitoring to show the contractor's procedures produce acceptable piles; several types suit CFA or DD piles, mostly technologies already used on drilled shafts; see O'Neill and Reese (1999) and DFI (2005). (p. 183)
key_points: Integrity tests supplement installation monitoring (p. 183).
sections.applicability: Post-installation integrity testing and load testing program for CFA pile quality assurance

sections.title: Use of Integrity Testing
sections.summary: Integrity results need experienced interpretation; acceptance is the design engineer's decision. Testing best verifies the control parameters; coring can check suspected defects. Typically 10% to 20% of production piles plus all test piles, more where experience is limited or problems expected; e.g., test the first 10 to 15 piles, then reduce if records match.
sections.body: Integrity tests need careful interpretation by experienced personnel, who cannot always tell whether an anomaly is a defect, so the design engineer decides acceptability from soil conditions, construction records, the integrity report and the possible effect on performance. Automated monitoring and control is the most reliable means of consistent QA/QC; integrity testing is best used to verify that the control parameters suit the site, and to evaluate piles that missed drilling or grouting criteria; coring can supplement or visually check suspected defects. Frequency is the owner's judgment: 10% to 20% of production piles is typical, plus all pre-production and verification test piles; more than 20% where agencies lack experience, conditions are difficult or problems are expected. A typical approach is to test the first 10 to 15 load-bearing piles, then keep, reduce or even eliminate testing if later records match. (p. 183)
key_points: Acceptance of an anomalous pile is the design engineer's decision (p. 183).
Integrity testing best verifies that installation control parameters suit the site (p. 183).
Typical frequency 10% to 20% of production piles plus all test piles (p. 183).
More than 20% where experience is limited or problems are expected (p. 183).
Test the first 10 to 15 piles, then adjust frequency by the records (p. 183).

sections.title: Integrity Testing by Surface Methods
sections.summary: Sonic echo, the common, cheap test from the pile top (Figure 7.11), is recommended for routine testing of CFA piles of 760 mm (30 in.) or less; reflections show impedance (EA/C) changes. Signals weaken beyond L/D of about 30, but the critical upper 6 m (20 ft) is well covered (Figure 7.12); defects under about 0.4 m (a quarter of the 1.6 m wavelength) go undetected.
sections.body: The sonic echo test is the most available, economical and easily applied integrity test, fast and without tubes, and is recommended for routine testing of CFA piles of 760 mm (30 in.) diameter or less. A small instrumented hammer strikes the pile top (Figure 7.11); the wave reflects from anomalies or the tip back to a receiver; reflections show changes in section or material, governed by impedance EA/C (E modulus, A area, C wave velocity); bulges and necks raise or lower impedance, and density changes may indicate defects; impulse response and impedance logging are other processing methods; a reflection before 2L/C suggests an impedance change above the toe (p. 184). The signal weakens with depth, so for depth-to-diameter ratios over 30 the toe and deep defects will likely go undetected; but the upper 6 m (20 ft) is most critical for CFA structural capacity (shear and moment), where sonic echo is most reliable, making it useful for testing many piles (Figure 7.12). Defects shorter than about 0.25 of the wavelength are generally not detected; a typical hammer gives about 1.6 m (5.3 ft), so anomalies under 0.4 m (15 to 16 in.) thick go undetected, appropriate for most CFA diameters (p. 185). (pp. 184 to 185)
key_points: Sonic echo recommended for routine testing of CFA piles of 760 mm (30 in.) or less (p. 184).
Pile impedance = EA/C; a reflection before 2L/C suggests an anomaly above the toe (p. 184).
Toe and deep defects likely undetected for depth-to-diameter ratios over 30 (p. 185).
Upper 6 m (20 ft) most critical for CFA structural capacity (p. 185).
Defects under about 0.4 m (15 to 16 in.) thick go undetected (1.6 m wavelength) (p. 185).

sections.title: Integrity Testing using Downhole Techniques
sections.summary: Downhole tests (crosshole and single-hole sonic logging, gamma-gamma; Figures 7.13, 7.14) are the most reliable but costly, recommended for unusually high moments or piles over 760 mm (30 in.). Tubes about 0.3 m apart inside the cage: Schedule 40 steel for CSL (PVC debonds), PVC for gamma. Tubes must be pushed into fluid grout.
sections.body: Down-tube tests (crosshole sonic logging CSL, single-hole sonic logging SSL, backscatter gamma) are the most reliable for anomalies in cast-in-place foundations, but given their difficulty and cost are recommended for piles with unusually high moments and/or diameters over 760 mm (30 in.). CSL measures wave speed between a source and receiver in two tubes; SSL (Figure 7.13) uses one probe, sampling material around the tube, a missing-arrival zone (5 to 6 m in the figure) suggesting a defect. Gamma-gamma logging (Figure 7.14) counts backscattered photons to give density within about 100 mm (4 in.) of the tube. Tubes for CSL or gamma should be evenly spaced about 0.3 m (1 ft) around the inside of the cage; CSL tubes should be Schedule 40 steel, which stays bonded (PVC debonds within days of set, defeating CSL); gamma needs PVC because steel blocks the photons. Tubes are attached to the steel before insertion, harder in CFA piles where they must be pushed into fluid grout, and testing is costlier and slower than sonic echo (p. 186). (pp. 186 to 187)
key_points: Downhole tests recommended for unusually high moments or diameters over 760 mm (30 in.) (p. 186).
Gamma-gamma measures density within about 100 mm (4 in.) of the tube (p. 186).
Access tubes about 0.3 m (1 ft) apart around the inside of the cage (p. 186).
CSL tubes Schedule 40 steel (PVC debonds); gamma tubes PVC (p. 186).

sections.title: Load Testing
sections.summary: Load testing is very important for CFA piles, both pre-production and verification (Figure 7.15): it verifies design parameters (allowing lower safety factors), sets drilling and grouting baselines and refines correlations. CFA capacities of a few hundred tons suit rapid or dynamic proof tests; proof testing does not harm a sound pile, which can be used.
sections.body: Load testing is a very important component of effective CFA pile use, as pre-production and verification tests (Figure 7.15); axial compression tests are most common, with uplift and lateral tests where those loads matter; both pre-production and verification tests should be integral to transportation projects (Section 7.3.5). Benefits: site data verify design parameters and increase reliability, which may allow lower ASD safety factors; the program sets baseline drilling rate and pressure/volume relations, grout flow and admixtures; results refine side and base resistance correlations. Ultimate capacities are generally no more than a few hundred tons, so rapid (Statnamic, Fundex) or dynamic (drop hammer) methods suit proof tests, which are generally not detrimental to a sound pile, so tested piles may be used in service. Detailed methods: Kyfor et al. (1992) FHWA-SA-91-042; Hannigan et al. (2006) FHWA-NHI-132021; Sabatini et al. (2005) FHWA NHI-05-039; O'Neill and Reese (1999) FHWA-IF-99-025. (p. 188)
key_points: Pre-production and verification load tests should be integral to CFA transportation projects (p. 188).
Site load test data may allow lower ASD factors of safety (p. 188).
CFA ultimate capacities generally not larger than a few hundred tons (p. 188).
Proof testing is generally not detrimental to a sound pile, which may be used in service (p. 188).

sections.title: Considerations in Planning a CFA Pre-Production Test Pile Program
sections.summary: A pre-production test program measures site resistance, ties it to construction methods and verifies design, especially for proprietary DD systems (also setting torque and downthrust targets). Test locations must represent the site with subsurface data at each. Static top-down tests are easy; a control static test with calibrated rapid or dynamic tests is efficient, always with a site-specific correlation.
sections.body: A pre-production program aims to (a) measure site-specific resistance, (b) correlate it to construction methods and (c) verify design assumptions (p. 188), particularly for DD piles with proprietary tooling; baseline drilling and placement parameters, and for displacement piles torque and downthrust targets, come from successful test piles. Test locations must represent the dominant site conditions, with subsurface information at each; one test pile may do for uniform soil and loads, otherwise several. CFA resistances suit conventional top-down static tests with contractor-built reactions; calibrated rapid or dynamic tests add speed and economy; on large projects a single control static test supplemented by several rapid or dynamic tests on the control and other piles gives maximum benefit at least cost; a site-specific correlation between static and rapid or dynamic tests should always be established (p. 189). (pp. 188 to 189)
key_points: Pre-production tests set baseline drilling and grouting parameters, and torque and downthrust for DD (p. 189).
Test pile locations must represent dominant site conditions, with subsurface data at each (p. 189).
Large projects: one control static test plus several rapid or dynamic tests (p. 189).
Always establish a site-specific correlation between static and rapid or dynamic tests (p. 189).
sections.applicability: Post-installation integrity testing and load testing program for CFA pile quality assurance

sections.title: Proof Tests on Production Piles
sections.summary: Modest CFA capacities make proof testing of production piles viable: rapid and dynamic tests are economical up to about 5 MN, printed as (450 tons) (Figure 7.16), several piles a day, supporting lower safety factors. Tests do not harm piles within structural capacity; a second load cycle is stiffer (Figure 7.17), which matters when comparing test methods on the same pile.
sections.body: The modest axial resistance of CFA piles and available rapid and dynamic methods make proof testing of production piles a viable QC/QA option, on random or questionable piles; rapid and dynamic tests are quite economical up to around 5 MN, (450 tons) as printed (Figure 7.16), with several piles a day once mobilized. Proof testing can support the higher reliability and lower factor of safety (or higher resistance factor) of load tested projects, with significant savings. Axial tests do not harm a pile whose structural capacity is not exceeded: in Figure 7.17 two cycles each reached a geotechnical limit (the first by Davisson, which generally gives conservative results), the second stiffer than the first; so a production load test does not impair later loading, and multiple tests can stiffen a CFA pile (p. 189), which matters when comparing a rapid or dynamic test with a static test on the same pile, the second test seeing a stiffer response (p. 190). (pp. 189 to 191)
key_points: Rapid and dynamic proof tests economical up to around 5 MN, printed as (450 tons) (p. 189).
Proof tests support lower factors of safety and cost savings (p. 189).
Load tests do not harm a pile whose structural capacity is not exceeded (p. 189).
A second load cycle gives a stiffer response; consider this when comparing methods on one pile (pp. 189 to 190).

sections.title: Summary of Recommended QC/QA Procedures
sections.summary: Section 7.7 summarizes the recommended QC/QA procedures for CFA pile projects as inspection checklists: before construction, equipment review, drilling, grouting, reinforcement and top finishing, and post-installation.
sections.body: This section summarizes recommended QC/QA procedures for CFA pile projects with checklists for inspection (7.7.1 to 7.7.6). (p. 191)
key_points: Checklists in 7.7.1 to 7.7.6 (p. 191).
sections.applicability: Checklist of recommended QC/QA and inspection procedures for CFA pile construction

sections.title: Prior to Construction
sections.summary: Before construction the experienced inspector reviews plans and specifications, the geotechnical report, the approved installation plan, load test details, monitoring requirements and control parameters, mix design and testing requirements, and reinforcement, top finishing and cutoff details.
sections.body: The inspector must be prepared and experienced in CFA techniques and, before construction, have and review: plans and specifications; the geotechnical report or other subsurface information; the contractor's approved installation plan; load test or pre-production test pile details; automated monitoring requirements and control parameters; grout or concrete mix design and sampling and testing requirements; and reinforcing details, pile top finishing and cutoff levels. (p. 191)
key_points: Review the approved installation plan and monitoring control parameters before construction (p. 191).
Review mix design, sampling and testing requirements (p. 191).
sections.applicability: Checklist of recommended QC/QA and inspection procedures for CFA pile construction

sections.title: On-site Review of Contractor’s Equipment
sections.summary: On arrival the inspector reviews equipment against the plans and installation plan: confirms the day's work and sampling party, documents auger diameter, length and pitch, each truck, reinforcement and centralizers, checks calibration and recording intervals, and checks equipment condition.
sections.body: On arrival the inspector reviews the contractor's equipment for compliance with plans, specifications and the installation plan: check in on the day's work and confirm the grout/concrete sampling party is present; document auger diameter, length and pitch, each truck on delivery, reinforcement type and configuration and centralizers; check calibration of volume monitoring and other equipment and that recording intervals are set; check equipment condition and tolerances. (p. 192)
key_points: Document auger diameter, length and pitch (p. 192).
Check calibration of volume monitoring and recording depth intervals (p. 192).
sections.applicability: Checklist of recommended QC/QA and inspection procedures for CFA pile construction

sections.title: During Drilling
sections.summary: During drilling confirm location and plumbness tolerances, the plug at the auger tip, pile identity and requirements, verticality or batter, cuttings and advance rate consistent with the reports, removal of spoil around the auger, and, at test piles, watch for subsidence or grout loss.
sections.body: During drilling: confirm location within horizontal tolerance and plumbness within range; confirm the plug at the auger tip; confirm which pile is being built so subsurface conditions and requirements (number, embedment, cutoff, batter) can be referenced; document verticality or batter, cuttings and advance rate, consistent with the geotechnical, test pile and load test reports; confirm removal of excessive spoil around the auger; during test pile construction watch the pile and ground for subsidence or loss of fluid grout. (p. 192)
key_points: Confirm the plug at the auger tip (p. 192).
Document advance rate and cuttings against the geotechnical and test pile reports (p. 192).
sections.applicability: Checklist of recommended QC/QA and inspection procedures for CFA pile construction

sections.title: During Grout/Concrete Placement
sections.summary: During grouting document mix properties and samples, start of pumping, initial volume and pressure head, and withdrawal rate; confirm the target minimum grout factor along the pile and the depth of first return. After a discontinuity the contractor may re-drill full length; re-drilling less than full length is generally unacceptable. Confirm steady pull, total volume and a clean pile top.
sections.body: During placement: document grout/concrete properties (batch time, temperature, additives, flow) and strength samples per specification; document immediate start of placement, initial volume and pressure head and withdrawal rates per the installation plan, and confirm from monitoring that the target minimum grout factor is reached along the pile (p. 192); document the depth of first grout return, consistent with the reports; if a discontinuity in return or other questionable condition appears, inform the contractor and note it; the contractor may re-drill the pile full length, and re-drilling less than the full length to restart grouting is generally considered unacceptable (compare the common practice in 7.4.2 of re-drilling 1.5 m below a pressure drop); confirm continuous steady pull (slow positive rotation if approved) with pumping until the tip leaves the ground; document total volume and overall grout factor; obtain the automated records; confirm the top is clear of debris and contaminated material (p. 193). (pp. 192 to 193)
key_points: Confirm the target minimum grout factor is attained along the pile (pp. 192 to 193).
Document the depth at which grout return is first observed (p. 193).
Re-drilling less than the full length to restart grouting is generally considered unacceptable (p. 193).
Pump until the auger tip leaves the ground; document total volume and grout factor (p. 193).
sections.applicability: Checklist of recommended QC/QA and inspection procedures for CFA pile construction

sections.title: During Reinforcement Placement and Pile Top Finishing
sections.summary: During reinforcement and top finishing document reinforcement against design and any difficulties (re-drilling and re-grouting is usually the most cost-effective remedy), confirm clean, rust-free bars with the specified extension above cutoff, and proper top finishing and tie-off.
sections.body: During reinforcement placement and pile top finishing: document reinforcement against the design; document installation difficulties, which may indicate obstructions or inclusions, re-drilling and re-grouting being generally the most cost-effective remedy for suspect conditions; confirm reinforcement is free of spoil or rust; confirm the specified extension above cutoff; confirm top finishing per requirements, including forms above grade and tie-off details. (p. 193)
key_points: Re-drill and re-grout is generally the most cost-effective remedy for suspect conditions (p. 193).
Confirm reinforcement extension above cutoff (p. 193).
sections.applicability: Checklist of recommended QC/QA and inspection procedures for CFA pile construction

sections.title: Post-Installation
sections.summary: After installation check grout subsidence and the cutoff, and see that integrity or proof tests are done promptly and questionable or rejected piles reported to the owner; Chapter 8 gives guide specifications.
sections.body: Post-installation: check for grout subsidence; inspect the cutoff; ensure integrity or proof load tests are scheduled and performed promptly and questionable or rejected piles are noted and reported to the owner and its engineer. Further details are in the project specifications; Chapter 8's guide specifications may serve as a starting point for state DOT specifications. (p. 193)
key_points: Check for grout subsidence after installation (p. 193).
Report questionable or rejected piles to the owner and its engineer (p. 193).
